methods.name: strong-lensing time-delay cosmography (TDC)
methods.details:
Distance:
The optical paths differ in length and gravitational potential, leading to a temporal difference in arrival time.
The time delay is measured by comparing the light curves of multiple images.
High-resolution imaging together with an assumed lens model or velocity dispersion helps to reduce mass-sheet degeneracy, hence constrain the Fermat potential differences.
Spatially resolved kinematics provide additional constraints to reduce the mass-anisotropy degeneracy.
The time-delay distance can be calculated from the Fermat-potential differences and time delay.
Redshift:
Spectroscopic redshifts of the lens and source obtained using absorption or emission lines are used.

methods.name: dispersion measure (DM)-z relation
methods.details:
FRBs' observed DM includes contributions from the 'local' Universe (ISM and halo), the intergalactic medium (IGM), and the host galaxy.
By dedispersion, the total DM can be obtained from the dynamic spectrum.
The 'local' Universe contribution is subtracted using a Galactic electron-density model. The host-galaxy DM contribution is separated out by jointly fitting with other parameters.
The resulting intergalactic-medium DM-z relation (Macquart relation) constrains $H_0$.

methods.name: gravitational wave (GW) bright siren
methods.details:
Distance:
The GW waveform's amplitude and phase jointly provide the chirp mass and luminosity distance, though distance is degenerate with the binary's inclination angle. This degeneracy can be reduced either by additional EM information (e.g. afterglow or jet imaging) or additional GW detectors with different orientations.
Velocity:
A detected EM counterpart allows identification of the host galaxy. Its spectroscopic redshift gives the source redshift, which is corrected for the host galaxy's peculiar velocity to obtain the recession velocity.

target.description: compact object merger (with EM counterpart) (BNS, NSBH)

methods.name: gravitational wave (GW) galaxy-catalog dark siren
methods.details:
Distance:
The GW waveform's amplitude and phase jointly provide the chirp mass and luminosity distance.
Redshift:
Every galaxy from a pre-existing catalog that lies within the GW 3-D localization volume is treated as a possible host and weighted by a completeness/luminosity model.
Marginalising over this galaxy redshift distribution and combining it with the GW luminosity-distance posterior into an $H_0$ posterior.
Combining multiple dark sirens narrows the combined $H_0$ posterior.

methods.name: gravitational wave (GW) spectral siren
methods.details:
Distance:
The GW waveform's amplitude and phase jointly provide the chirp mass and luminosity distance.
Redshift:
There are identifiable features in the source-frame mass spectrum of black holes (e.g. the pair-instability mass gap), which allow the redshift to be inferred by comparing the detector-frame and assumed source-frame masses.

methods.name: gravitational wave (GW) tidal siren
methods.details:
Distance:
The GW waveform's amplitude and phase jointly provide the chirp mass and luminosity distance.
Redshift:
Neutron stars experience tidal deformation during inspiral.
Tidal deformation parameters can be inferred from the GW phase evolution; combined with an assumed equation of state, this yields the source-frame mass.
Comparing the detector-frame and source-frame mass then determines the redshift.

methods.name: gamma-ray attenuation
methods.details:
Gamma-ray photons from blazars pair-produce with EBL photons while propagating over cosmological distances, attenuating the observed spectrum in an energy- and redshift-dependent way.
Comparing observed blazar spectra against an assumed intrinsic spectral shape yields the observed optical depth.
The same optical depth can also be predicted theoretically, by combining EBL density and path length to that redshift, which depends on $H_0$.
Fitting the predicted and observed optical depth constrains $H_0$.

methods.name: SZ decrement + X ray
methods.details:
Distance:
The Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect (SZE) arises from inverse Compton scattering of CMB photons by hot ICM electrons and is characterised by the Compton parameter $y \propto \int n_e T_e\, d\ell$.
The X-ray bremsstrahlung surface brightness scales approximately as $S_X \propto \int n_e^2 \Lambda(T_e)\, d\ell$.
Given an assumed ICM model and temperature, the different density dependences of the SZE and X-ray signals allow the line-of-sight physical scale to be constrained. Together with angular radius, $D_A(z)$ can be obtained.
Redshift:
Spectroscopic redshifts of cluster member galaxies are used to determine the cluster systemic redshift.

methods.name: megamaser
methods.details:
Distance:
Water masers in the edge-on accretion disk around compact object follows Keplerian orbital motion.
Observed velocities with long-term acceleration monitoring in a disk model yields a purely geometric angular-diameter distance to the host galaxy.
Velocity:
Host-galaxy spectroscopic redshifts are used, with corrections for peculiar velocities.

methods.name: expanding photosphere method (EPM)
methods.details:
Distance:
The photosphere radius grows via free expansion.
The angular size, calculated from the observed flux and color temperature, is corrected by the dilution factor.
Angular size and photospheric velocity inferred from the spectrum are then fitted to obtain the distance.
Redshift:
Host-galaxy spectroscopic redshifts of host galaxies are used, with corrections for peculiar velocities.

methods.name: cosmic chronometers (CC)
methods.details:
For an FLRW metric the Hubble parameter obeys $H(z) = -\frac{1}{1+z}\frac{dz}{dt}$.
The $4000\,\text{\AA}$ break measured from galaxy spectra is calibrated with stellar population synthesis models to infer stellar population ages.
Measuring the age difference $dt$ between two passive-galaxy populations separated by a small redshift interval $dz$ yields $H(z)$ directly.
Reconstructing or extrapolating $H(z)$ to $z=0$ gives $H_0$.

methods.name: spectroastrometry and reverberation mapping (SARM)
methods.details:
Distance:
SA resolves the photocenter displacement of the BLR across velocity channels, giving its angular size.
RM measures the light-travel-time lag between the AGN continuum and broad-line flux variations, giving the linear size of the BLR.
Jointly fitting a parameterized BLR model to the RM and SA data yields a purely geometric angular-diameter distance to the AGN.
Redshift:
Spectroscopic redshift of the AGN (host galaxy)

methods.name: cosmic microwave background (CMB)
methods.details:
The CMB angular power spectrum encodes the sound horizon at recombination $r_s$ as a physical ruler. The acoustic peak positions measure its angular scale $\theta_*=r_s/D_A(z_*)$.
Within an assumed early-universe physics and a flat $\Lambda$CDM parameterization, jointly fitting the full power spectrum (peak heights and angular scale) constrains $\Omega_m h^2$, $\Omega_b h^2$ and $\theta_*$.
$H_0$ is then derived as one output of this global parameter fit.

methods.name: baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) + Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN)
methods.details:
Distance:
The BAO feature originates from acoustic waves in the pre-recombination photon-baryon plasma and provides a standard ruler given by the sound horizon at the drag epoch $r_d$.
Large spectroscopic surveys measure galaxy clustering through the correlation function or power spectrum, which constrain transverse ($D_M(z)​/r_d$) and radial ($D_H(z)/r_d$) distance ratios.
BBN measurements of primordial D/H abundance constrain baryon density, which calibrates $r_d$.
These measurements together yield $D_M(z)$ and $H(z)$.
Redshift:
Spectroscopic redshifts of large-scale structure tracers are used.

methods.name: equality scale from CMB lensing
methods.details:
The matter power spectrum features a turnover at $k_eq$ (the matter-radiation equality scale).
This turnover is imprinted on the lensing power spectrum in the form of $k_{\rm eq}\chi_* \propto \Omega_m^{0.6}\,h$, since the CMB lensing power spectrum is primarily determined by the line-of-sight projection integral of the matter power spectrum.
Using a prior on $A_s$ and an external measurement of $\Omega_m$, $H_0$ can be constrained.

facility.description: high-resolution CMB survey telescope (Planck; ACT, SPT; Simons Observatory)

methods.name: parallax
methods.details:
Distance:
Earth's orbit around the Sun produces an apparent angular displacement of nearby stars relative to distance background stars.
Measuring the parallax angle over multiple epochs allows the geometric distance to be determined using the 1 AU baseline.

target.description: first-rung distance indicators in the Milky Way

methods.name: detached eclipsing binary (DEB)
methods.details:
Distance:
Spectroscopy measures the radial velocity semi-amplitudes. Combined with theorbital period and inclination angle constrained by the light curve, the orbital semi-major axis $a$ can be determined. Togther with the relative radii $R_1/a$ and $R_2/a$ from light-curve modelling, the physical radii are obtained.
Photometry provides colour information, from which surface brightness is inferred using the surface brightness-colour relation. This yields the angular diameters.
Combining the physical and angular sizes gives the geometric distance.

methods.name: Cepheids
methods.details:
Distance:
The pulsation period of a Cepheid correlates with stellar radius and mass, which, together with the narrow temperature range of Cepheids, produces a tight relation between period and luminosity.
Measuring the pulsation period and extinction-corrected apparent magnitude allows the intrinsic luminosity and distance to be determined.

methods.name: tip of the red giant branch (TRGB)
methods.details:
Distance:
Low-mass red giant stars (RGB) reach TRGB at a nearly fixed helium-core mass before the helium flash, producing a sharp cutoff in the RGB luminosity function.
Photometry is used to construct a color–magnitude diagram, and the TRGB magnitude is determined from the luminosity-function discontinuity using edge detection or luminosity-function fitting, with corrections for extinction and color/metallicity dependence.
Comparing the observed TRGB magnitude with its geometrically calibrated absolute magnitude yields the distance modulus and hence the distance.

facility.description: high-resolution, deep imaging photometry of uncrowded halo fields (e.g. HST, JWST)

methods.name: J-region asymptotic giant branch (JAGB)
methods.details:
Distance:
Carbon-rich thermally-pulsing AGB stars occupy a distinct region of near-infrared color–magnitude diagrams and have a relatively narrow luminosity function in the J band.
Near-infrared photometry is used to color-select JAGB stars and determine a characteristic apparent magnitude from their luminosity function using the mode or other statistics.
Comparing this apparent magnitude with a geometrically calibrated JAGB absolute magnitude yields the distance modulus and hence the distance.

facility.description: near-IR imaging photometry (e.g. JWST/NIRCam; ground-based near-IR imagers)

methods.name: Mira variables
methods.details:
Distance:
Mira variables are fundamental-mode pulsating asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars that follow a period–luminosity relation (PLR). Shorter-period ($P<400$ days), oxygen-rich Miras exhibit a particularly tight near-infrared PLR.
This population is selected using period, amplitude, and crowding criteria to minimize systematic effects.
Multi-epoch near-infrared photometry provides the pulsation period and intensity-averaged mean magnitude, which, combined with the calibrated PLR, yields the distance.

methods.name: flux-weighted gravity-luminosity relation (FGLR)
methods.details:
Distance:
Blue supergiant stars cross the HR diagram at nearly constant luminosity and mass, producing a tight relation between bolometric luminosity and the 'flux-weighted gravity' $g_F=g/T_{\rm eff,4}^4$.
Spectroscopically determining a blue supergiant's effective temperature, gravity, and metallicity gives its luminosity via the FGLR.
Combining with extinction-corrected multi-band photometry yields the distance.

methods.name: Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia)
methods.details:
Distance:
Brighter SNe Ia have broader light curves and decline more slowly after peak brightness.
SNe Ia light curves are fitted to obtain peak magnitude, light-curve stretch, and color parameters. These parameters are used to standardize SN Ia luminosities through light-curve shape and color corrections, together with host-galaxy and selection-bias corrections.
The standardized magnitudes are then converted into luminosity distances using the calibrated SN Ia absolute magnitude.  
Velocity:
Host-galaxy spectroscopic redshifts of Hubble-flow SNe Ia are used, with corrections for peculiar velocities.

methods.name: Type II Supernovae (SNe II)
methods.details:
Distance:
Intrinsically brighter SNe II have higher expanding photophere velocity.
Multi-band photometry of SNe II provides the apparent magnitude and colour, while optical spectroscopy measures the expansion velocity from absorption features. These quantities are used to correct the SNe II luminosity.
The corrected luminosities are then converted into luminosity distances using the calibrated SN II absolute magnitude.
Velocity:
Host-galaxy spectroscopic redshifts are used, with corrections for peculiar velocities.

methods.name: surface brightness fluctuations (SBF)
methods.details:
Distance:
The further a galaxy is, the more stars are averaged within each resolution element, making its surface brightness smoother.
The fluctuation variance is measured from the Fourier power spectrum and normalized by the mean galaxy flux to obtain the fluctuation flux, which is converted into the apparent SBF magnitude.
The absolute SBF magnitude is corrected for stellar-population dependence using the galaxy color and calibrated with first-rung distance indicators; together with the apparent magnitude, it yields the distance.
Velocity:
Group-averaged CMB-frame recession velocities derived from spectroscopic redshifts are used.

methods.name: Tully-Fisher relation (TF)
methods.details:
Distance:
The luminosity of a rotation-supported spiral galaxy correlates with its rotation velocity, which is inferred from the inclination-corrected H I linewidth.
The relation's slope is constrained by galaxy clusters and its zero point is calibrated using the previous rung.
Comparing the corrected apparent magnitude with the inferred absolute magnitude yields the distance.
Velocity:
CMB-frame recession velocities derived from spectroscopic redshifts are used, with peculiar velocities reduced by group/cluster averaging or flow modelling.

methods.name: fundamental plane (FP)
methods.details:
Distance:
Early-type galaxies follow an empirical Fundamental Plane relating their physical effective radius, mean surface brightness, and stellar velocity dispersion. Imaging provides the angular effective radius and mean surface brightness, while spectroscopy provides the stellar velocity dispersion.
After calibrating the FP relation using the previous rung, the physical effective radius can be calculated.
Comparing the physical and angular effective radius yields the angular-diameter distance.
Velocity:
CMB-frame recession velocities derived from spectroscopic redshifts are used.

methods.name: HII L-σ relation
methods.details:
Distance:
The HII galaxies and giant HII regions are empirically found to follow a common relation between H$\beta$ luminosity and the velocity dispersion of the ionised gas.
The relation's zero point is calibrated using giant HII regions in nearby galaxies with independently measured distances.
The measured velocity dispersion predicts the intrinsic H$\beta$ luminosity, which, when compared with the spectrophotometrically measured H$\beta$ flux, yields the luminosity distance.
Velocity:
Spectroscopic redshifts of Hubble-flow H II galaxies.

methods.name: gamma-ray bursts (GRB)
methods.details:
Must be calibrated against a low-redshift probe (commonly SNe Ia distance moduli via Gaussian-process interpolation, or cosmic chronometers H(z)).
Distance:
$L_{\rm peak}$ is obtained from the gamma-ray (prompt emission) light curve, $L_a$ and $T_a^*$ are obtained from the X-ray (afterglow) light curve.
The 3D Dainotti fundamental plane combines three observables into a single correlation, used to standardize the GRB's intrinsic luminosity so it can serve as a distance indicator.
Redshift:
Spectroscopic redshift is used.
